title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Problem served: E506 explains and extends Lagrange's 1766–69 method for separated equations dx/√X = dy/√Y. Lagrange introduces a parameter t, puts dx/dt = √X and dy/dt = √Y, differentiates twice and forms combinations of x+y and x−y that integrate. In §§11–15 Euler applies the idea to the non-radical equation dx/X = dy/Y with X = a+2bx+cx². He obtains the complete algebraic integral (a+b(x+y)+cxy)/(x−y) = const and shows the computation breaks down once cubic terms are added.

Top of this page (end of §15). Already the simple cubic case dx/(1+x³) = dy/(1+y³) admits no algebraic integral. On each side the integral is (1/3)ln(1+x) − (1/6)ln(x²−x+1) + (1/√3)·arctan((2x−1)/√3), a mixture of logarithms and circular arcs. These are transcendentals of different kinds that cannot be compared. An algebraic relation F(x) − F(y) = C is possible only when each side involves transcendentals of a single kind.

Analysis heading: the sign-changed equation dx/(a+2bx+cx²) + dy/(a+2by+cy²) = 0.

§16. Put dx/X = dt and dy/Y = −dt. Euler says repeating the previous calculation gives nothing. After weighing the difficulties he found an artifice that adds a not-negligible increment to Lagrange's method.

§17. From dx/dt = X and dy/dt = −Y he forms (y dx + x dy)/dt = yX − xY. With u = xy this gives du/dt = a(y−x) + 2bxy − 2bxy + cxy(x−y) = a(y−x) + cxy(x−y). Setting q = x−y, du/dt = q(cu−a).

Continued on the next page. Dividing gives c du/((cu−a)dt) = cq. Differentiating the defining equations gives ddx/(dt dx) = X' and ddy/(dt dy) = −Y', whose sum is X' − Y' = 2c(x−y) = 2cq. Subtracting twice the logarithmic equation and integrating yields dx·dy/(cu−a)² = C dt². Hence XY/(a−cxy)² = const, i.e. (a+2bx+cx²)(a+2by+cy²)/(a−cxy)² = C. The test case a=c=1, b=0 recovers arctan x + arctan y = arctan((x+y)/(1−xy)).

Modern view of the artifice. The substitution y = a/(cw) gives dy/(a+2by+cy²) = −dw/(a+2bw+cw²). This Möbius involution reduces the '+' case to the '=' case already solved. Substituting w = a/(cy) into the earlier integral XW/(x−w)² gives exactly ac·XY/(cxy−a)². So u = xy is in effect the invariant of this involution, and a − cxy plays for the minus sign the role that x − y (or a+b(x+y)+cxy) plays for the plus sign.
errors: No mathematical errors in the computations on this page: yX − xY = (y−x)(a − cxy) is correct, and so is du/dt = q(cu−a).

§15's claim that any such equation of degree above two admits no algebraic integral is stated too generally. It holds for generic cubics. Degenerate polynomials (e.g. a perfect cube (x−r)³, or other repeated-root cases) give rational integrals, and then algebraic relations exist. The 'single kind of transcendental' criterion is heuristic and not proved.
Latin agreement slip in the print: 'quantitates transcendentes diuersos' should read 'diuersas'.

Euler's description of the artifice as a genuine increment to Lagrange's method is somewhat overstated. The minus case reduces to the plus case by the elementary substitution y → a/(cy), which Euler does not mention.

ideas.what: Heuristic: an algebraic integral of dx/P(x) = dy/P(y) requires that the transcendental parts (logs vs arctangents) be of one kind; cubic denominators mix kinds and so admit no algebraic integral.
ideas.modern_name: Linear independence of logarithms / Liouville–Ritt-type criteria for algebraic relations among elementary integrals
ideas.usually_credited_to: Abel, Liouville (1830s); Ritt, Rosenlicht (20th c.) for rigorous forms
ideas.where_published: E506 itself; similar remarks recur in Euler's papers on comparison of transcendentals (unsure of exact loci)

ideas.what: Lagrange-style parametrisation for the sign-reversed Riccati-type separated equation, using the auxiliary product u = xy to obtain a logarithmic differential, then the integral XY/(a−cxy)² = C.
ideas.modern_name: Integration of dx/Q(x) + dy/Q(y) = 0 via a Möbius involution preserving Q(x)⁻¹dx up to sign; invariant u = xy
ideas.where_published: E506, Nova Acta / Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. (published early 1780s); Opera Omnia I.21 (unsure of exact volume)

missed.claim: The 'artifice' u = xy is equivalent to the Möbius involution y ↦ a/(cy), which sends dy/(a+2by+cy²) to −dw/(a+2bw+cw²). It therefore reduces the new case to §13. Euler presents it as a new extension of Lagrange's method without noting this group-theoretic reduction. This prefigures the view of such integrals as orbits of the projective group preserving a quadratic form.
missed.quote: tandem in artificium incidi, quo hunc caſum expedire licuit
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of minor historical-pedagogical interest. It illustrates how Lagrange's parametric trick encodes symmetries of the differential, a point probably obvious to any commentator.

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains a correct, routine extension of Lagrange's method, already published in E506 itself, plus a known heuristic about mixed transcendentals. Nothing appears absent from the record.
